questions.solution: Correct Option B - Increased serum parathyroid hormone: This patient has resistant hypertension despite treatment with three antihypertensive drugs , which should raise concerns for secondary hypertension. Additionally, she suffers from nephrolithiasis , weakness , fatigue , nausea , and decreased appetite . Primary hyperparathyroidism , a known cause of secondary hypertension , is characterised by elevated serum parathyroid hormone . Patients with primary hyperparathyroidism can exhibit recurrent nephrolithiasis , nausea, decreased appetite, fatigue , and weakness in addition to having hypercalcemia and hyperparathyroidism . By altering vascular reactivity and preventing day-night blood pressure regulation , hypercalcemia is thought to contribute to hypertension . Primary hyperparathyroidism is also a common finding in MEN 1 and MEN 2A. Pheochromocytoma , another potential (concurrent) cause of secondary hypertension that should be taken into account in this patient, is frequently associated with MEN 2A. However, it typically also manifests with central obesity, thin and easily bruisable skin, abdominal striae, and proximal muscle atrophy. Option C - Increased serum aldosterone-to-renin ratio: An elevated serum aldosterone-to-renin ratio indicates primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome). Primary hyperaldosteronism can cause secondary hypertension with features of hypokalemia (e.g., fatigue and muscle weakness). However, this patient's potassium level is normal. Moreover, hypercalcemia and symptoms such as recurrent renal stones or gastrointestinal complaints are not expected in Conn syndrome. Option D - Decreased thyroid-stimulating hormone: Decreased serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) would indicate hyperthyroidism, which is an important cause of treatment-resistant secondary hypertension and may present with weakness and fatigue. Hyperthyroidism could also explain this patient's hypercalcemia, as thyroid hormones have osteoclastic activity. questions.solution: Correct Option A - 25-hydroxycholecalciferol → 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol: This patient's symptoms ( fatigue, weakness, constipation, decreased appetite, and intermittent flank pain , likely due to kidney stones ) and laboratory abnormalities ( increased calcium and parathyroid hormone , decreased phosphorus ) are consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism. In primary hyperparathyroidism , the excessive parathyroid hormone causes the proximal convoluted tubule cells of the kidney to express 1-alpha-hydroxylase , which boosts the conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol into its metabolically active form, 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. Cholecalciferol is converted from 7-dehydrocholesterol , which was previously synthesised in the skin under the influence of sunlight, to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol in the liver. Loss of 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity would cause this stage of vitamin D metabolism to slow down in kidney disease , resulting in a vitamin D deficiency. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cholecalciferol → 25-hydroxycholecalciferol: The conversion of cholecalciferol to 25-hydroxy cholecalciferol by 25-hydroxylase takes place in the liver. It is stimulated by a higher substrate availability due to increased intake (e.g., from dietary supplements) or endogenous production of cholecalciferol, not by excess parathyroid hormone in primary hyperparathyroidism. Option C - 25-hydroxycholecalciferol → 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol The deactivation of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol occurs in the kidneys and is stimulated by high concentrations of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. Parathyroid hormone impairs this step by decreasing the activity of the responsible enzyme, 24-hydroxylase. Option D - 7-dehydrocholesterol → cholecalciferol: The conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) takes place in the skin under the influence of ultraviolet B (UVB) rays. This enzymatic reaction is stimulated by exposure to sunlight, not by excess parathyroid hormone in primary hyperparathyroidism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Iodine deficiency: In the case above, the 5-month-old patient has clinical features including retarded growth, dry skin, poor head control, coarse face, umbilical hernia and goitre . The patient in this clinical scenario has congenital hypothyroidism caused by iodine deficiency . Iodine is a necessary component of the thyroid hormone . Iodine deficiency is a major in congenital hypothyroidism worldwide, particularly in iodine-deficient countries . Severe iodine lack leads to hypothyroidism, which impairs somatic growth and motor development in children. Moderate to severe iodine deficiency results in multifocal autonomous thyroid growth and thyrotoxicosis. Due to a lack of iodine, iodine-induced congenital hypothyroidism is characterised by severely stunted development and cerebral abnormalities . Dry skin, a protruding tongue, and a distended abdomen are also major characteristics. Growth may not always be normal, even with thyroid hormone replacement , since many newborns cannot absorb the hormone. Incorrect Options: Option B - Growth hormone deficiency: Growth hormone deficiency (GHD), commonly referred to as dwarfism or pituitary dwarfism , is a disorder characterised by low levels of growth hormone in the body . GHD children have unusually small heights but acceptable body proportions. Another good factor of growth retardation is hypothyroidism . The prognosis for height in children with late-diagnosed congenital hypothyroidism is uncertain. Option C - Enzymatic defect: A condition caused by an enzyme deficiency (functional abnormalities). Newborns are frequently screened for enzyme abnormalities such as galactosemia and phenylketonuria (PKU). Albinism and phenylketonuria are two disorders caused by enzyme deficiencies . Option D - Pituitary tumour: A pituitary tumour is a growth that occurs inside the pituitary gland . Pituitary tumours can cause central hypothyroidism by compacting pituitary thyrotrophs, resulting in a decrease in TSH secretion . @Neet_pg_bot

Treatment options for Riedel's thyroiditis are limited, and there is no consensus on a standard approach. Oral corticosteroids, such as prednisone, are often prescribed to treat Riedel's thyroiditis. Corticosteroids have potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, which can help to reduce the inflammation and fibrosis associated with Riedel's thyroiditis. However, long-term use of corticosteroids can have side effects, including weight gain, osteoporosis, and an increased risk of infection. Therefore, corticosteroids in Riedel's thyroiditis are typically reserved for cases where other treatments have failed, and the benefits outweigh the risks. Other treatments for Riedel's thyroiditis may include tamoxifen, methotrexate, or surgical removal of the affected tissue . Treatment is tailored to the individual patient based on their symptoms and disease severity. Treatment with corticosteroids is generally recommended to prevent complications such as tracheal compression, dysphagia, and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy . Myxedema coma is a rare and life-threatening complication of severe, untreated hypothyroidism. Low blood pressure Low blood sugar Hypoxia, hypercapnia, hypernatremia, and sluggish heartbeat. This leads to a range of symptoms, including fatigue, weakness, weight loss, low blood pressure, and darkening of the skin. Addison's disease can also cause a life-threatening condition called an adrenal crisis, which can result in shock and multiple organ failure. This leads to an increase in metabolic rate, causing symptoms such as weight loss, rapid heartbeat, anxiety, and tremors. In severe cases, hyperthyroidism can lead to a life-threatening condition called thyroid storm , which can cause fever, delirium, rapid heart rate, and organ failure. When a high concentration of calcium binds , the serum level of PTH is decreased. Binding of PTH to the receptor results in the activation of cyclic AMP (cAMP)-dependent G-protein. Laboratory tests reveal a serum calcium level of 8.5 mg/dL (normal range: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL), a serum phosphate level of 4.5 mg/dL (normal range: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL), and an elevated serum PTH level of 90 pg/mL (normal range: 10-65 pg/mL). What is the cause of these clinical findings?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Secondary hyperparathyroidism: Based on these findings, the patient has secondary hyperparathyroidism , a condition that often develops in patients with CKD (chronic kidney disease) due to impaired renal function. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is an excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) due to an underlying disease or condition that affects calcium and phosphate metabolism. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is one of the most common causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism. In CKD , there is a decline in the kidney's ability to excrete phosphate and activate vitamin D, which leads to a decrease in calcium absorption from the intestine. This results in hypocalcaemia (low blood calcium) and hyperphosphatemia (high blood phosphorus). The parathyroid glands sense this low calcium state and respond by producing more PTH to maintain calcium homeostasis The increase in PTH levels causes calcium and phosphorus to be released from the bones , which leads to bone resorption and decreased bone mineral density . PTH activates vitamin D , which increases c alcium and phosphate absorption from the intestine and helps to maintain normal serum calcium levels However, the persistent elevation of PTH levels can lead to adverse effects, including Renal osteodystrophy, Bone pain Fractures Vascular calcification. Therefore, treatment of secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD is essential to maintain the balance of calcium and phosphate and prevent complications Treatment options Vitamin D analogues Phosphate binders Calcimimeticswhich can help to lower PTH levels and improve calcium and phosphorus metabolism. In severe cases , surgery to remove the parathyroid glands may be necessary to control hyperparathyroidism. Incorrect Options: Option A - Primary hyperparathyroidism: Primary hyperparathyroidism is a disorder in which there is excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) from one or more of the parathyroid glands, leading to hypercalcemia (high blood calcium) and hypophosphatemia (low blood phosphate). In most cases, parathyroid adenoma develops in one of the parathyroid glands. The excess PTH secretion led to increased calcium reabsorption from the bones and enhanced renal calcium reabsorption , which raises blood calcium levels. Symptoms including fatigue, weakness, muscle and bone pain , kidney stones, and cognitive changes. Option C - Hypervitaminosis D: Hypervitaminosis D, also called vitamin D toxicity, o ccurs when there is an excessive intake of vitamin D leading to high levels of vitamin D in the body . This can be caused by taking high doses of vitamin D supplements or by excessive sun exposure. Symptoms of hypervitaminosis D can include nausea, vomiting, constipation, dehydration, frequent urination, weakness, fatigue, and confusion Option D - Hypoparathyroidism: In Hypoparathyroidism, parathyroid glands secrete too little parathyroid hormone (PTH) . PTH is important for regulating calcium and phosphorus levels in the body. When PTH levels are low , calcium levels in the blood decrease and phosphorus levels increase. questions.solution: Correct Option A - 1 alpha-hydroxylase: Vitamin D is activated by the enzyme of 1 alpha-hydroxylase that is present in the kidney under the action of PTH. Its main function is to stimulate calcium reabsorption from the kidney and absorption from the gastrointestinal tract. However, indirectly it can activate vitamin D mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule by stimulating the 1-alpha hydroxylase enzyme. questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with DiGeorge syndrome is being evaluated during a routine follow-up. While discussing the case with medical students, the doctor asks about the hormones involved in regulating blood calcium levels. Which of the following hormones is responsible for this function?
questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy with DiGeorge syndrome is being evaluated during a routine follow-up. While discussing the case with medical students, the doctor asks about the hormones involved in regulating blood calcium levels. Which of the following hormones is responsible for this function?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Parathormone: Parathormone or parathyroid hormone is the major polypeptide involved in regulating extracellular Calcium and phosphate levels. Parathyroid hormone is secreted mainly from chief cells of parathyroid glands located behind each pole of the thyroid gland. Calcium ion concentration in the extracellular fluid is the strongest stimulus for the secretion of parathyroid hormone, which is detected by a calcium-sensing receptor in parathyroid cell membranes. The calcium-sensing receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor that, when stimulated by high extracellular calcium ions decreases PTH secretion via inositol triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG) pathway. There are many mechanisms by which increased parathyroid hormone exerts its effect in low calcium ion concentration states: Effect of Parathyroid hormone on the bones: Parathyroid hormone stimulates bone resorption by binding to its receptors on osteoblasts, stimulating synthesis of receptor activator for nuclear factor κ-B ligand ( RANKL ). RANKL binds to its receptor (RANK) and stimulates the differentiation of pre-osteoclastic cells into mature osteoclasts. Mature osteoclasts possess the ability to remodel the bones by dissolution and degradation, releasing Calcium into the blood. Effect of parathyroid hormone on the kidneys: Parathyroid hormone increases renal tubular reabsorption of Calcium and decreases reabsorption of phosphate The increased calcium reabsorption occurs mainly from distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts. Conversely, decreased reabsorption of phosphate ions occurs at proximal convoluted tubules . Effect of parathyroid hormone on the small intestine: Parathyroid hormone exerts its effect on calcium homeostasis indirectly by stimulating the production of 1 alpha-hydroxylase in the proximal convoluted tubule , which converts inactive 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to active vitamin D – 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. Active vitamin D, in turn, increases the absorption of Calcium from the intestine through transcellular and paracellular pathways Incorrect Options: Option B - Tetraiodothyronine: Thyroxine or tetraiodothyronine(T4) and triiodothyronine(T3) are thyroid hormones known for controlling growth, cellular metabolism, and other body functions . Though thyroid hormones play an essential role in children’s growth, they do not play an important role in maintaining blood calcium levels. Option C - Prolactin: Prolactin is a peptide hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. It promotes secretion, milk production, and mammary gland development . It has no role in maintaining adequate extracellular calcium ion concentration. Option D - Cortisol: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid secreted by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex . It is also known as a stress hormone . Glucocorticoids play a very important role in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism. Cortisol at high levels can increase bone resorption despite that it has no effect on calcium homeostasis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - 1-alpha-hydroxylase: 1-alpha-hydroxylase is a mitochondrial cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for catalysing the conversion of vitamin D into its active form. It is the most tightly regulated step in the synthesis of Vitamin D, influenced by several factors, including; PTH and low phosphate levels, which stimulate it and 1,25-(OH)2D3, which suppresses it Parathyroid hormone is the major regulator of 1-alpha-hydroxylase. Any drop in plasma calcium concentration stimulates the secretion of PTH, which in turn increases the synthesis of 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the kidneys. Mutation in 1-alpha-hydroxylase decreases vitamin D activation, as can be seen in vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 , an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by the early onset of rickets and low plasma calcium. Incorrect Options: Option A - 25-hydroxylase: 25-hydroxylase is a cytochrome P450 enzyme present in the endoplasmic reticulum of the liver, where it catalysts the formation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D, also called calcidiol . It is not regulated by PTH. Option C - 5-alpha-reductase: 5-alpha-reductase is involved in the conversion of testosterone into dihydrotestosterone in target tissues; it does not participate in calcium homeostasis. Option D - 17-alpha-hydroxylase: 17-alpha-hydroxylase catalyses the conversion of pregnenolone and progesterone into their 17-hydroxy forms , an important step in synthesising cortisol and sex hormones. It does not participate in Vitamin D metabolism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Ribosome: Given the physical examination findings and past medical history, this patient likely has hypocalcemia secondary to parathyroid hormone deficiency . 22q11 deletion syndrome, or DiGeorge syndrome, is a congenital condition characterised by wide phenotype expression variability. Dysmorphic facial features, cleft palate, congenital heart defects, thymic hypoplasia, and hypoparathyroidism are among the commonest associations with the syndrome. The ribosomes first synthesise parathyroid hormone as a preprohormone , a polypeptide chain of 110 amino acids. Upon further processing, in the endoplasmic reticulum, the preprohormone is cleaved down to a pro hormone with 90 amino acids and then finally to the hormone itself with 84 amino acids in the Golgi apparatus . The parathyroid hormone is then sent to its destination site, packed in tiny secretory granules. 60-70% of PTH is degraded in the liver by Kupffer cells , while the remaining is degraded in the kidneys and, to a lesser extent, in other organs. Incorrect Options: Option A - Mitochondria: Mitochondria is a double membrane-bound cellular organelle. Even though oxyphil cells are abundantly filled with numerous, often large and blizzard mitochondria, giving it the characteristic dense eosinophilic colour under a microscope, it has no role in synthesising parathyroid hormone. Option C - Golgi Apparatus: Golgi apparatus is involved in processing and packaging molecules, especially those proteins which are destined to be exported out of the cell. Pro-PTH, which contains 90 amino acids, enters the Golgi apparatus, where it is converted into the parathyroid hormone. Ribosomes synthesise the parathormone peptide, which undergoes processing, packaging and transportation via the Golgi apparatus. Option D - Endoplasmic reticulum: The endoplasmic reticulum cleaves the pre-pro-PTH synthesised from ribosomes present on its surface into a prohormone called pro-PTH. Despite its role in polypeptide processing, ribosomes are the primary organelles involved in the synthesis of PTH. @Neet_pg_bot

Active vitamin D, in turn, increases the absorption of calcium and phosphate from the small intestine. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Calcitonin suppresses the secretion of PTH: Calcitonin is a peptide secreted from the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland. In many ways, calcitonin acts as an antagonist of the parathyroid hormone . Just as parathyroid hormone increases plasma calcium concentration by stimulating osteoclastic resorptive activity, in the same manner, calcitonin decreases serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts and release of parathyroid hormone . Although there is no direct effect of calcitonin on parathyroid hormone, but it can act indirectly to inhibit its secretion; Calcitonin can indirectly inhibit the secretion of parathyroid hormone by binding to its receptors on osteoclasts , thereby preventing the breakdown of bone tissue and the release of calcium into the blood, thus activating the negative feedback loop responsible for parathyroid hormone regulation. Conversely, when the calcium levels are low, parathyroid hormone secretion increases, and calcitonin levels decrease. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Psammoma bodies: In the abovementioned case, the patient has clinical features, including thyroid nodule, weight loss, and a histology picture showing psammoma bodies. All these features suggest papillary cell carcinoma is a likely possibility. Psammoma bodies are concentric, lamellated, calcified structures frequently seen in the papillary structures of the tumour and are thought to be a hallmark feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma but may also be seen in other types of malignancies. They are the most recognisable histologic feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Papillary thyroid cancer is distinguished by several distinguishing histologic characteristics in addition to psammoma bodies, such as ground-glass or "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei, which are larger nuclei with a transparent or pale appearance result of chromatin margination. Papillary thyroid cancer is also frequently associated with nuclear grooves , cytoplasmic invaginations of the nuclear membrane, and intranuclear pseudo inclusions , cytoplasmic invaginations within the nucleus. These histologic characteristics aid in distinguishing papillary thyroid carcinoma from other thyroid cancers and benign lesions, which helps to inform therapeutic therapy and the patient's prognosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - Amyloid deposition: Amyloid deposition is not a characteristic feature of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Instead, it is typically observed in medullary thyroid carcinoma , associated with calcitonin-derived amyloid deposition in the stroma. Option C - Sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm: Sheets of tiny cells do not indicate papillary thyroid cancer with little cytoplasm. This histologic pattern is more frequently linked to small cell carcinoma , a neuroendocrine tumour that is extremely aggressive and poorly differentiated. Option D - Trabecular pattern with hyalinised stroma: Papillary thyroid cancer does not typically have a trabecular appearance with hyalinised stroma. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Total thyroidectomy with central compartment neck dissection: As mentioned above, the patient's clinical features include a palpable thyroid mass with FNAC showing amyloid deposits. These findings are suggestive of medullary cell carcinoma. A total thyroidectomy with central compartment neck dissection is the best treatment for this patient because the tumour is 3 cm in diameter, and lymph nodes are implicated. Whereas central compartment neck dissection removes the lymph nodes in the central compartment of the neck, where MTC frequently metastasizes, a total thyroidectomy removes the entire thyroid gland, including the tumour. This surgical strategy removes the original tumour and affected lymph nodes completely, lowering the chance of recurrence and improving the patient's prognosis. A modified radical neck dissection may also be considered in cases of extensive lymph node involvement or extrathyroidal extension . Following surgery, the patient's serum calcitonin levels should be monitored to assess the operation's success and detect any potential recurrence. Adjuvant therapies, such as external beam radiation or targeted therapies , may be considered for patients with residual disease or a high risk of recurrence. Incorrect Options: Option A - Lobectomy: Lobectomy , which involves the removal of only one thyroid lobe, is insufficient for managing MTC, especially in cases with lymph node involvement . Total thyroidectomy with central compartment neck dissection is the preferred surgical approach for this patient. Option C - Radioactive iodine ablation: Radioactive iodine ablation is ineffective for MTC , as this tumour type does not concentrate on iodine. It is typically used as adjuvant therapy for patients with differentiated thyroid cancers, such as papillary and follicular thyroid carcinoma. Option D - Chemotherapy: Chemotherapy is generally not the first-line treatment for MTC. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Compression of the trachea: Compression of the trachea is the most commonly associated complication with medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). As the tumor grows and invades surrounding tissues , it can compress or displace nearby structures, such as the trachea and esophagus, leading to symptoms like shortness of breath, cough, and difficulty swallowing. The extent of compression depends on the size and location of the tumor , as well as the involvement of other neck structures. In severe cases, the compression can lead to airway obstruction , necessitating urgent intervention, such as a tracheostomy. Furthermore, local invasion and compression can also affect the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness or vocal cord paralysis. Early diagnosis and appropriate surgical management , such as total thyroidectomy with central compartment neck dissection, can help prevent or alleviate compression-related complications in MTC patients. It can occur when the parathyroid glands are inadvertently damaged or removed during thyroidectomy, leading to low parathyroid hormone levels and hypocalcemia. ATC is often characterised by rapid growth, invasion of surrounding tissues, and distant metastasis, making obtaining a timely and accurate diagnosis important. FNAB involves inserting a thin needle into the thyroid nodule and extracting a sample of cells for analysis. This sample can then be examined for characteristic features of ATC , such as pleomorphic giant cells, spindle cells, and multinucleated giant cells. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): The patient presents with the clinical features of a transient hyperthyroid phase of De Quervain's thyroiditis (subacute thyroiditis). It usually affects females 20-40 years of age. It occurs due to transient thyroid gland inflammation after infection with Coxsackie, mumps, or adenovirus. The inflammation results in the release of stored thyroid hormones resulting in a transient hyperthyroid state for the initial 4-6 weeks . The resulting damage to the follicular cells impairs the synthesis of new thyroid hormones and causes transient hypothyroidism until normal thyroid function is restored within 4-6 months. The patients present with a painful thyroid gland. The pain radiates to the angle of the jaw and the ears and is made worse with swallowing, coughing, and neck movement . Systemic symptoms are also common. Physical examination reveals an enlarged and tender thyroid gland. Investigations show raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). In the thyrotoxic phase, iodine uptake is low. Treatment involves us ing non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and a beta-blocker for pain and systemic upset. Some patients may need prednisolone 40mg daily for 3-4 weeks. Incorrect Options: Option B - Propylthiouracil: Propylthiouracil is an antithyroid drug. It acts by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase, thus inhibiting the iodination of tyrosine. It also prevents the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. It is used for patients presenting with hyperthyroidism and Graves’ disease. In subacute thyroiditis, antithyroid drugs are useless as thyroid hormone synthesis is already impaired. Prescribing antithyroid drugs to these patients will prolong the resulting hypothyroid state later. questions.stem: A 30- year-old female presented in an outpatient department due to complaints of perioral tingling, numbness, and muscle cramps for 2 days. On physical examination, there was a transverse healing scar on her neck. Light tapping over the angle of the jaw resulted in the twitching of the ipsilateral facial muscles. Which of the following changes in serum chemistry might be expected in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 30- year-old female presented in an outpatient department due to complaints of perioral tingling, numbness, and muscle cramps for 2 days. On physical examination, there was a transverse healing scar on her neck. Light tapping over the angle of the jaw resulted in the twitching of the ipsilateral facial muscles. Which of the following changes in serum chemistry might be expected in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Low serum calcium levels: The patient presents with tingling, numbness, muscle cramps, and positive Chvostek’s sign along with a neck scar indicating that she likely has hypoparathyroidism and hypocalcaemia secondary to thyroid surgery . During thyroid surgery, the surgeon may inadvertently remove or damage the parathyroid glands present behind the poles of the thyroid gland, leading to a decrease in the production of parathyroid hormone . This can result in low serum calcium levels and high serum phosphate. Parathyroidectomy results in a steady decline of serum calcium concentration, and the symptoms of hypoparathyroidism usually develop 2-3 days postoperatively, but in some cases, they may not appear for weeks. Tingling or numbness in the hands, feet, or around the mouth, muscle cramps, fatigue, and seizures are among the commonest manifestations of hypocalcaemia. Clinically on the bedside, hypocalcaemia can be diagnosed by eliciting two important signs, including: Chvostek's sign : contraction of the ipsilateral facial muscles, following a tap over the facial nerve at the angle of the jaw. Trousseau's sign : A painful, involuntary contraction of upper extremity muscles resulting in the flexion of the wrist and thumb with an extension of the fingers. It can be elicited by blocking the blood circulation with a blood pressure cuff inflated above systolic pressure for a few minutes. Inadequate calcium levels can lead to hyperexcitability of the nerves and muscles , causing them to contract spontaneously in response to a stimulus. Incorrect Options: Option A - Low serum phosphate levels: Parathyroid hormone is very important in regulating serum calcium and phosphate ion concentration. As seen in this patient, lower levels of parathyroid hormone secondary to parathyroidectomy result in low serum calcium and elevated serum phosphate levels. Low phosphate levels can be seen in hyperparathyroidism, alcoholism, and malnutritio n. Option B - High serum calcitonin levels: Calcitonin is a peptide hormone secreted from the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland in response to a high calcium concentration . Calcitonin and parathyroid hormone work in an antagonising fashion to maintain calcium homeostasis. This patient will have low serum calcitonin levels instead due to thyroidectomy. Option D - High serum parathyroid (PTH) levels: A higher serum parathyroid hormone level results in a higher serum calcium concentration , which is usually presented with symptoms of flank pain, muscle weakness, lethargy, constipation, depression, anxiety, hallucinations, and psychosis . As this patient presented with hypocalcaemia features, one or more parathyroid glands were removed during thyroid surgery leading to low PTH and serum calcium levels. @Neet_pg_bot
